sets.t: Renal, Liver, Cardiac & Adrenal Function Tests: Essay questions
Renal, Liver, Cardiac & Adrenal Function Tests: MCQs

exam: A 35‑year‑old woman with weight gain, purple striae, and hypertension presents for routine check‑up. What is the first test you would order? — Morning serum cortisol and ACTH to screen for Cushing syndrome.

A 28‑year‑old man with fever, hypotension, and confusion is admitted. He has a history of chronic steroid use. What is the most urgent management step? — Immediate IV hydrocortisone and fluids to treat possible adrenal crisis.

A patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency presents with a urinary tract infection. What adjustment should you make to his steroid regimen? — Increase hydrocortisone dose to stress dose (double or triple) during infection.

A 50‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient on antiretroviral therapy develops fatigue and low blood pressure. Which test would help differentiate adrenal insufficiency from drug side effects? — Morning serum cortisol and ACTH stimulation test.

A patient with suspected Cushing syndrome has a normal short‑acting ACTH test but elevated urinary free cortisol. What is the next step? — Perform a low‑dose dexamethasone suppression test to confirm autonomous cortisol production.
A patient with adrenal tuberculosis presents with hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Primary adrenal insufficiency due to adrenal destruction by TB.
ai.title: Adrenal Function Tests
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Adrenal function tests assess cortisol production, ACTH responsiveness, and adrenal steroid synthesis to diagnose insufficiency, excess, or adrenal pathology. Clinicians interpret results with clinical context, especially in resource‑limited settings.

sections.p: Adrenal function tests evaluate the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑adrenal (HPA) axis, determining whether the adrenal glands produce adequate cortisol and respond to ACTH stimulation.

t.b: < 5 µg/dL suggests insufficiency; > 18 µg/dL suggests excess or stress.
Low ACTH with low cortisol = secondary; high ACTH with low cortisol = primary.

b: Severe adrenal insufficiency: cortisol < 5 µg/dL, hypotension, hyponatraemia.
sections.p: Adrenal insufficiency is staged by cortisol levels, clinical severity, and response to stress. Cushing syndrome severity is gauged by urinary cortisol and clinical features.
In low‑resource settings, infections, tuberculosis, HIV, malaria, schistosomiasis, and herbal remedies are common precipitants.

Adrenal insufficiency presents with fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia. Cushing syndrome shows central obesity, purple striae, hypertension, and glucose intolerance.
Baseline labs plus targeted endocrine tests guide diagnosis. When tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and empirical therapy are essential.

t.b: Na < 135 mmol/L or K > 5.0 mmol/L suggests AI.

sections.p: Life‑threatening complications include adrenal crisis, septic shock, and severe hypoglycaemia. Prompt recognition is vital.
Treat underlying cause, replace cortisol, and monitor electrolytes. Avoid drugs that inhibit cortisol metabolism and use non‑steroidal anti‑inflammatories cautiously.

t.b: Chosen for its short half‑life and low mineralocorticoid potency in secondary AI.
Avoid in secondary AI where aldosterone is adequate.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of cortisol response, electrolytes, and blood pressure. Prevent infections and educate on stress dosing.
Adrenal insufficiency mimics sepsis, hypoadrenalism, and chronic fatigue; Cushing syndrome mimics metabolic syndrome.

b: Cortisol rise in acute illness may mask AI
sections.p: Stress, infection, or recent steroid use can elevate cortisol; low ACTH may be due to assay interference.
